title: File handling
specPoints: 2.2.3 **File handling operations**: open, read, write, close
learn: Explain why programs store data in files (persistence between runs)
Open a file for reading, writing and appending, and explain the difference between `w` and `a`
Read a file line by line until the end, and process each line
Write lines to a file, remembering newlines and closing the file
Read and write OCR pseudocode file operations in exam questions
hook: Your quiz program keeps a high score — until you close it. Then it's gone. Every real program remembers things after it ends: scores, settings, your essay. Memory forgets when the power goes; files don't.

video.title: Files: how programs remember
video.brief: 4 minutes. RAM as a whiteboard wiped when the program ends; a file as a notebook on the shelf. Open the notebook (open), read line by line with a finger moving down until the end (endOfFile), close it. Then writing: `w` tears out all the pages first, `a` writes on the next blank page. Show a scores file growing with `a`. End with the OCR four-step pattern and the Python `with open(...) as f:` block side by side.

p: Variables live in RAM and vanish when the program ends. A **file** on secondary storage keeps data between runs: high scores, user settings, a list of customers. Text files are just lines of characters, which is why you read and write them line by line.

explain.code:
OCR pseudocode                              Python
myFile = open("scores.txt")                 file = open("scores.txt", "r")
while NOT myFile.endOfFile()                for line in file:
    print(myFile.readLine())                    print(line.strip())
endwhile                                    file.close()
myFile.close()
                                            # or, safer: closes automatically
                                            with open("scores.txt") as file:
                                                lines = file.readlines()
after: Each line read is a **string** including its newline; cast with `int()` after `.strip()` if it's a number. OCR's `endOfFile()` loop is the exam pattern — know it.

explain.code:
OCR pseudocode                              Python
myFile = open("scores.txt")                 file = open("scores.txt", "w")   # w: wipes, starts fresh
myFile.writeLine("Ada,95")                  file.write("Ada,95\n")          # add \n yourself
myFile.close()                              file.close()

newFile("log.txt")   # creates empty file    file = open("scores.txt", "a")   # a: adds to the end
after: `"w"` **overwrites** the whole file; `"a"` **appends**. Choosing `w` when you meant `a` deletes every previous score — a favourite exam question. Always close the file (or use `with`) so the data is actually saved.

p: Files often hold several fields per line separated by commas: `Ada,95`. Split the line (`line.split(",")`), cast the parts, then use them. To find the highest score: read every line, split, compare — the max-finding loop from 2.2.8 applied to a file.
explain.code:
best = 0
with open("scores.txt") as f:
    for line in f:
        name, score = line.strip().split(",")
        if int(score) > best:
            best = int(score)
            best_name = name
print(best_name, best)

simple.h: Files keep data after the program ends
p: Variables are forgotten when the program stops. A file is saved on the disk and is still there next time.

simple.h: Reading: open, read each line, close
simple.code:
file = open("scores.txt", "r")
for line in file:
    print(line.strip())
file.close()

simple.h: Writing: w starts fresh, a adds on
simple.code:
file = open("scores.txt", "a")   # a = add to the end
file.write("Ada,95\n")           # \n = new line
file.close()
after: `"w"` deletes everything first. `"a"` keeps what is there. Always close the file.

simple.code:
myFile = open("scores.txt")
while NOT myFile.endOfFile()
    print(myFile.readLine())
endwhile
myFile.close()

keyterms.def: Opening, reading, writing and closing files from a program.
Open a file to read from it; the file must exist.
Open a file to write; creates it, or erases existing contents.
Open a file to add to the end without erasing.
The point after the last line; `endOfFile()` becomes true.
Finish using a file so data is saved and resources released.

exam.q: Write an algorithm that reads every line from the file `names.txt` and outputs the number of lines in the file.
model: Opens the file (1). Loop that continues until end of file — `while NOT file.endOfFile()` / `for line in file` (1). Reads a line and increments a counter inside the loop (1). Closes the file and outputs the count (1).
exam.commentary: The close is a mark. In OCR pseudocode the `endOfFile()` loop is expected; a Python `for line in file` is accepted. Counting before reading, or reading twice per iteration, loses the loop mark.

exam.q: A program saves a player's score using `file = open("scores.txt", "w")`. Explain why previous scores are lost and how to fix it.
model: Write mode overwrites / erases the existing contents when the file is opened (1). Open in append mode (`"a"`) instead so new scores are added to the end (1).
exam.commentary: Name the mode and its effect; name the fix.

exam.q: The file `temps.txt` contains one temperature per line. Write an algorithm that outputs the highest temperature in the file.
model: Opens the file and initialises highest (1). Loops until end of file (1). Reads each line, converts to a number and compares with highest, updating when larger (1). Closes the file and outputs highest (1).
exam.commentary: Casting the line to a number is the subtle mark — comparing strings gives wrong answers ("9" > "10"). Initialise highest from the first line or a very low value.

home: Write a simple diary: a menu that lets the user add an entry (appended to `diary.txt` with today's date typed in), show all entries, or search entries for a word. Hand in the code and a screenshot of the file after three entries.
